procedural_history.impugned_order: First order granting stay passed on 23rd June 2023 and the second order dated 22nd May 2024 granting liberty to the appellant to apply for interim bail.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court initially granted an ex-parte stay of the bail order on June 23, 2023.  The application for cancellation of bail was listed on 24-25 dates from 23rd June 2023 to July 2024. One learned Single Judge, after reserving the judgment, recused himself. After that, two other learned Single Judges recused themselves. The application to vacate the stay was repeatedly adjourned. The High Court order dated 22nd May 2024, regarding the application to vacate the stay, was also problematic.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's orders of June 23, 2023 and May 22, 2024, preferred appeals to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court, on June 7, 2024, stayed the High Court's stay order of June 23, 2023, and clarified that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the bail order granted by the Special Court on June 17, 2023. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the appeals.

directions: The impugned orders by which the High Court granted the stay of the order granting bail are set aside.
Pending the hearing of application for cancellation of bail, the order dated 17th June, 2023 passed by the Special Court will continue to operate.
All the contentions on the merits of the application for cancellation of bail are expressly left open to be decided by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an interim stay on an order granting bail, particularly when the stay was granted ex-parte, without recording reasons, and in a case that was not rare or exceptional.

facts: The High Court granted an ex-parte interim stay on an order that had granted bail to the accused.
The High Court did not record any reasons for its conclusion that this was a rare and exceptional case warranting such a drastic order.
Although the advocate for the accused was present, the High Court did not hear them before granting the stay.
This ex-parte stay order remained in effect for over a year, during which the application for cancellation of bail was listed 28 times without a decision on the stay.
The original bail order had found that the accused made out a case for bail, and there were no subsequent allegations of misuse of liberty.
law: The power to grant an ex-parte interim stay of a bail order should not be used as a normal rule; it must be exercised only in very rare and exceptional cases.
When granting such a stay, the court is duty-bound to record specific reasons explaining why the case is exceptional and warrants such a drastic measure.
A stay on a bail order requires a very strong prima facie case for the cancellation of bail to be made out.
If an ex-parte stay is granted, the court has a duty to immediately hear the accused on the continuation of the interim relief, as the right to liberty under Article 21 is involved.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had granted the stay mechanically, without applying its mind to the merits or considering if the case was truly exceptional.
The High Court's failure to record any reasons for the stay was a direct violation of its duty.
By not hearing the advocate for the accused, the High Court rendered an unjustified ex-parte order, which was further vitiated by the failure to record reasons.
The Court noted that the case was not rare or exceptional, especially since the grounds for cancellation were on the merits of the original bail order, not on any new conduct by the accused.
The fact that the stay continued for a year without hearing the accused on the merits was deemed a serious violation of the appellant's fundamental right to liberty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting the interim stay. It held that the failure to hear the accused, the failure to record reasons, and the mechanical application of such a drastic power in a non-exceptional case vitiated the High Court's order. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned orders of the High Court that had stayed the grant of bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting an interim stay on an order granting bail, particularly when the stay was granted ex-parte, without recording reasons, and in a case that was not rare or exceptional.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court improperly granted an ex-parte interim stay on the bail order.
The appellant pointed out that this interim stay was continued from time to time over several months (from August to November 2023) without the matter being fully heard.

The appellant contended that the High Court failed to record any reasons for granting such a drastic ex-parte stay, which is a mandatory requirement, especially as it should only be done in rare and exceptional cases.

cases.case_name: Gulabrao Baburao Deokar v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: An ex-parte stay of a bail order should not be granted as a normal rule and can be exercised only in rare and very exceptional cases. When such a drastic order is passed, the court is duty-bound to record reasons why it was a rare and exceptional case warranting the stay.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: As a normal rule, the ex-parte stay of a bail order should not be granted; this power can be exercised only in rare and very exceptional cases where the situation demands it.
obiter: The matter could not be heard due to paucity of time.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The power to grant an ex-parte ad interim stay on an order granting bail is a drastic measure that can only be exercised in rare and very exceptional cases. When a court chooses to exercise this power, it is duty-bound to record its reasons for concluding that the case was so exceptional as to warrant such an order, a requirement the High Court failed to meet in this instance.
legal_tests_applied: In an application for cancellation of bail, the power to grant an interim stay on the bail order can be exercised only in exceptional cases when a very strong prima facie case for cancellation is made out.
While granting a stay of an order of grant of bail, the Court must record brief reasons for coming to a conclusion that the case was an exceptional one and a strong prima facie case is made out.
As a normal rule, an ex-parte stay of a bail order should not be granted; this power can be exercised only in rare and very exceptional cases where the situation demands it.

When a court grants an ex-parte ad interim stay of a bail order, it is duty-bound to record reasons why it concluded that it was a very rare and exceptional case where such a drastic order was warranted.
Where a drastic ex-parte order of stay is passed, it is the duty of the Court to immediately hear the accused on the prayer for continuation of the interim relief.
policy_considerations: Granting an ex-parte stay of a bail order is a 'drastic order' that directly impacts the liberty of the accused, and therefore its use must be strictly limited to prevent procedural injustice.
The requirement for courts to record reasons for staying a bail order, especially an ex-parte stay, serves as a crucial safeguard to ensure that such a significant power is not exercised arbitrarily.

When a court passes a drastic ex-parte order affecting an individual's liberty, principles of fairness dictate that the court has a duty to immediately hear the affected party (the accused) on the continuation of that order.
